question: For a number of years, aircraft manufacturers have been calling for the flight deck crew to be reduced to a single pilot during the flight, apart from take-off and landing. They argue that the technology is so advanced that a single pilot can carry out the necessary tasks while the flight is in cruise phase, which would help mitigate the serious staffing shortages in airlines1.

The idea is met with strong opposition from pilot associations, who argue that automation technology will simply increase profits for aircraft manufacturers at the expense of pilot and passenger safety.

Despite the position taken by pilots, in 2021 the EU Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) launched a process to assess the possibility of implementing extended minimum crew operations (eMCO), which should be completed in 20272. 1.

Should the EASA not take into account the opposition from pilot organisations, which highlight the importance of pilots checking each other and of having a second pilot in the cockpit in case, for example, one pilot loses consciousness?

Is the Commission not concerned that reducing the number of pilots in a cockpit to one could deter young people from becoming pilots because of the increased responsibility involved and because they would not feel sufficiently safe?

In the Commission’s view, would the implementation of eMCO not have a negative impact on the training of new pilots, who would be deprived of the opportunity to fly with older and more experienced colleagues?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.4.2024) The Commission is aware of this initiative, which is currently being addressed by the European Union Agency for Aviation Safety (EASA) in two tasks.

The first is Rulemaking task RMT0739, which has just started and responds to a manufacturing industry initiative to develop technologies to allow the safe operation of large passenger aeroplanes by a single pilot during the cruise phase.

This task aims to produce an opinion by 2026 and has already identified pilots, aircraft operators, manufacturers, air navigation service providers and aviation authorities as entities that need to be involved. The second task is research task RES.0028 that seeks to develop a risk assessment framework for the main hazards associated with such a concept, including pilot incapacitation. 1.

In this work EASA has consulted and will consult broadly the various stakeholders, including pilots. The European Cockpit Association has been involved in discussions and in a working group on the topic since 2021. 2.

As regards the possible distrust of future pilots in the safety of the system, any new aircraft certification or procedures will not be approved unless they can be proven to provide at least an equivalent level of safety compared to today’s multi-crew operations. 3.

As regards the need for young pilots to gain experience with older pilots, this would only be marginally affected, as the initiative foresees retaining the two-pilot cockpit for the more demanding parts of the flight.
